Five types of AI agents: from reacting to learning

Not every agent remembers, pursues goals or learns. These everyday examples make their differences easier to understand.

By Juliana Gonzalez · September 29, 2026 · 6 min read

A motion-sensor light, a smart vacuum and a travel planner can all be understood as agents. They receive information and act, but they do not behave in the same way.

Some agents only react to what is happening now. Others keep information about their environment, pursue goals, compare alternatives or improve through experience.

A more complex system is not always a better system. The key is choosing the capabilities the problem actually needs.

1. Simple reflex agent

A simple reflex agent responds to the current situation through predefined rules. Its logic can be summarized as: if this happens, perform this action.

It does not remember what happened before, plan ahead or learn. Its behavior depends entirely on the input it receives at that moment.

Example: a motion-sensor light that turns on when it detects someone.

2. Model-based reflex agent

This agent also uses rules, but it maintains an internal representation of its environment. It keeps information about what has happened or about the system's current state.

Example: a smart vacuum that creates a map of the rooms, remembers the areas it has cleaned and detects which ones are still pending.

Memory helps it make better decisions, but remembering does not necessarily mean learning. The agent can use previous information without changing its behavior through experience.

3. Goal-based agent

A goal-based agent does more than react. It receives an objective and evaluates which actions will help it reach that objective.

Example: a travel agent that builds an itinerary according to the destination, dates and requested activities.

To complete the task, it needs to create a sequence, check different options and verify that the result meets the goal.

4. Utility-based agent

For some problems, reaching a goal is not enough because several solutions may be valid. A utility-based agent compares alternatives and tries to select the best result according to a set of criteria.

Example: a ride-sharing application that assigns a driver by considering distance, waiting time, price, availability and ratings.

The closest option may not be the fastest, and the cheapest may involve a longer wait. The decision depends on how each criterion is valued.

5. Learning agent

A learning agent uses previous experiences and outcomes to change its behavior. Instead of always executing the same rules, it incorporates feedback to improve over time.

Example: a writing assistant that adapts its suggestions according to which proposals a person accepts, edits or rejects.

Learning requires the system to observe what worked, receive an evaluation signal and adjust its approach.

A quick comparison

Simple reflex

Reacts to current input. Example: motion-sensor light.

Model-based

Maintains information about the environment. Example: vacuum with a map.

Goal-based

Plans to reach an objective. Example: travel agent.

Utility-based

Compares alternatives. Example: ride-sharing app.

Learning

Improves through experience and feedback. Example: writing assistant.

Memory, goals and learning are not the same

These capabilities are often confused, but they represent different functions:

  • An agent can retain information without learning from it.
  • It can pursue a goal without changing its strategy through experience.
  • It can compare alternatives without remembering previous decisions.
  • It can learn while also using goals, models or utility criteria.

In practice, many systems combine characteristics from several types. This classification helps identify the main capability guiding their behavior; it is not meant to place every system into a rigid category.

Choosing the right agent

Before designing an agent, it is worth asking whether it needs to remember information, reach a goal, compare alternatives or improve through feedback.

A simple automation can solve a predictable problem perfectly well, while other situations require planning, evaluation or learning.

The goal is not to build the most complex agent, but the right agent for the task.

This article draws on concepts studied in the IBM SkillsBuild Artificial Intelligence Fundamentals course. The explanations, structure and examples were developed and adapted for Julitree.
